newsitem.title: UK: Israeli nuclear arms vulnerable to attack - Jane's.
newsitem.headline: Israeli nuclear arms vulnerable to attack - Jane's.

text.p: Jane's Intelligence Review says Israel could be pushed into launching a pre-emptive nuclear strike because its nuclear arsenal is vulnerable to attack,

In an article to be published in its September issue and released to media in advance, the monthly military review argues Israel has failed to adapt its military strategy to the realities of the post-Soviet world, which has left its arsenal susceptible to a renegade nuclear attack.
"While Israel has implied that its undeclared nuclear arsenal would only be used in response to a nuclear -- or perhaps a chemical -- attack, the disposition of that arsenal suggests otherwise."

The report then asked: "Would an Israeli government be tempted to launch an attack rather than ride out a crisis...given the vulnerability of Israel's nuclear missiles -- and Israel's demonstrated willingness to strike when it perceives a threat?"

Using satellite imagery of the Zachariah missile base near Tel Aviv, Jane's said there were no missile storage silos that could withstand a nuclear blast because Israeli strategy during the Cold War was to retaliate immediately before the base was destroyed by incoming Soviet missiles.

The missiles and their launchers at the base, estimated to number about 150, are stored in hollowed out limestone caves which, according to the report, cannot be reinforced to provide sufficient protection.

"The vulnerability of the missile base appears to show an inertia within the Israeli military. Instead of renewing its nuclear strategy after the fall of the Soviet Union and focusing on making a nuclear deterrent that could survive an attack by Third World nuclear weapons, Israel continued to focus on producing more nuclear weapons as if envisioning a nuclear exchange with a geographically large country.
"Just a few nuclear-tipped missiles might neutralise Israel's missile threat and damage the nearby bunkers holding the air force's nuclear gravity bombs," the article said.
Israeli officials rarely comment on the country's nuclear arsenal other than to say that the Jewish state would not be the first to introduce such weapons into the region.
Jane's estimates Israel's arsenal to include more than 400 deliverable thermonuclear and nuclear weapons, which were first deployed in 1968 as a deterrent against the former Soviet Union.
